title: Reverence (IV.1)
hookLine: the fourth book is about receiving communion with reverence
tomorrow: what do you do when you can't get to the table?

lines: YOUR NAME IS ON THE INVITATION.
STILL, YOU STOP ON THE STEP.
cards: You're invited to dinner at a teacher's house, or your partner's parents', or a wedding where you barely know the couple. The invitation is real. Your name is on it.
And still, on the front step, you stop, fix your collar, and take a breath before you ring. Why hesitate at a door you're invited through?
Book four of the Imitation opens on exactly that front step, and it calls the pause reverence.

teach.h: COME TO ME, ALL YOU BURDENED.
teach.b: Book four is about communion, and it opens with a page of invitations in Christ's voice, gathered from the Gospels.
One reads, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." Then the disciple answers, and the first move isn't to run in. It's to stop.
You call me, and I'm a sinner, he says.
How do I dare? The chapter doesn't let either side win. The invitation stays.
The awe stays. Held together, that pair is reverence.

teach.h: ARKS AND A TEMPLE, MADE WITH CARE.
teach.b: Then he remembers people who took great care over signs of God's presence. Noah, working long on the ark. Moses, building an ark of wood for the tablets of the law.
Solomon, building the temple. If they took such care over signs, he asks, how should I prepare to receive the Lord himself?
Here's a line Catholics say at every Mass, right before communion, adapted from a Roman soldier in Matthew's Gospel: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof."
In the Gospel, Jesus marvels at the man's faith.
That's reverence in this book. Not hanging back, and not barging in. Coming, because the invitation is real, and coming carefully, because of who's inviting.

how: Before communion at Mass, Catholics say together a line adapted from the centurion in Matthew 8:8; the Church asks those receiving to fast for an hour beforehand, and some pray quietly afterward.

o: coming close to the holy with care and awe
a loud, joyful feeling during the music at Mass
staying away from church until you feel ready

games.q: book four's front step — tap the pairs.
p: great care over signs of God
a soldier's words, said at Mass

s: reverence means staying away until you feel worthy
the invitation stays. reverence is coming, and coming carefully.
the words before communion at Mass come from a Roman soldier in Matthew
the centurion: Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof.
book four says the awe should cancel the invitation
the chapter holds both together; that pair is what it calls reverence.

games.q: your friend is invited to be godmother at her cousin's baptism, and she says she's not holy enough to stand up there. what would book four say?
o: say yes, and prepare with care; the invite is real and so is the awe.
say no; if she doesn't feel worthy, she shouldn't come close.
say yes and don't overthink it; an invitation means nothing to prepare.
games.why: the disciple trembles at the door and still comes. Noah, Moses and Solomon show the care. reverence is both at once.

practice: Take a posture of arriving: sit up, set both feet flat, and fold your hands or rest them open on your knees. Bring to mind one thing you'd want to set right before coming close to something holy.
Then, if you pray, say the soldier's words slowly: Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof.

wordCard.voice: Reverence. In book four, the invitation to come close and the awe of who's inviting, held together.

orig.note: Latin: Lord, I am not worthy, the centurion's words (Matthew 8:8) as Catholics said them at the Latin Mass.

carryVoice: Your line: come with reverence. Not hanging back, and not rushing in either. Day 1489, done.
